one_liner: C# JSON serializer that emits per-type IL at runtime; ~3.4x faster serialization than Json.NET in a 2014 benchmark.
what_it_does: Maps .NET objects (classes, structs, lists, any IDictionary, Tuple, ExpandoObject, primitives) to and from JSON strings. The API is a static class: NetJSON.Serialize<T>(value) and NetJSON.Deserialize<T>(json), with TextWriter/TextReader, System.Type and NetJSONSettings overloads, plus DeserializeObject for an untyped Dictionary<string, object> tree. It is not a drop-in for Json.NET: the entry points differ, it has its own [NetJSONProperty] attribute and its defaults differ.
how_it_is_fast: The first time it sees a type, it generates a specialized serializer/deserializer class with System.Reflection.Emit (a TypeBuilder in one shared dynamic assembly plus DynamicMethod stubs) and caches it in a static generic field, so later calls do no reflection. The generated code appends into a StringBuilder cached per thread, formats integers with a 4-digit lookup table into stackalloc buffers (IntUtility), and deserializes by walking the string with unsafe char* pointers and hand-written number parsers. Property names are matched by a generated chain of string.Equals checks. It deliberately skips type validation: the author declined type-mismatch checks for performance (issue #217).
when_to_use: Hot paths that serialize small, statically typed POCOs through the generic Serialize<T>. In the author's .NET 5 BenchmarkDotNet run (issue #238, i7-8650U), a 2-property object took 219.8 ns vs 503.0 ns for System.Text.Json.
Legacy .NET Framework 3.5/4.0 code bases that need a faster JSON mapper than Json.NET. The 1.4.7 package still ships net35 and net40 builds.
Services that exchange JSON as .NET strings (UTF-16) rather than UTF-8 byte buffers.
Long-running processes with a fixed set of types, where the one-time IL-generation cost per type is paid back over many calls.
Trusted, well-formed payloads produced by your own systems.
when_not_to_use: Object-typed data such as Dictionary<string, object> with mixed values, or boxed values. A contributor's .NET 5 run in issue #238 measured NetJSON at 6.387 us vs 1.494 us for System.Text.Json on such a dictionary, and a boxed int at 937 ns vs 161 ns.

UTF-8 or stream pipelines such as ASP.NET Core request and response bodies. There is no byte[], Span, Stream or async API, and the TextReader overloads call ReadToEnd, so the whole payload is buffered (issue #232). Utf8Json beat NetJSON in the same #238 run (150.8 vs 219.8 ns).
Untrusted input. The parser skips type validation by design, and infinite loops on malformed JSON have been reported and fixed several times (#197, #217, #226).
High-precision decimal fields such as money: decimal values are parsed through a hand-written double parser (new Decimal(FastStringToDouble(...))), so digits beyond double precision are lost.
Native AOT, trimmed or other no-JIT targets: serializers are emitted with Reflection.Emit at runtime and there is no source generator.

integration.form: shared lib (NuGet package `NetJSON`, managed DLL). The library is five .cs files that need AllowUnsafeBlocks if you vendor them.
integration.dependencies: none on the net35 to net9.0 targets; the netstandard1.6/2.0 targets pull in the System.Reflection.Emit* packages, plus Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyModel on 1.6
integration.min_toolchain: .NET Framework 3.5, .NET Standard 1.6 or .NET 5. The 1.4.7 package ships net35, net40, net462, net472, netstandard1.6, netstandard2.0 and net5.0 through net9.0 builds.
integration.platforms: Any OS or architecture running a JIT-capable CLR with Reflection.Emit; the code uses unsafe pointers. Native AOT support is not documented, and it is unlikely to work because serializers are generated at runtime.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The caches are ConcurrentDictionary, type generation runs under locks, and the StringBuilders and settings are [ThreadStatic], so concurrent Serialize/Deserialize calls appear to be intended. The global static option setters are not synchronized.

gotchas: Defaults differ from Json.NET. SkipDefaultValue is true, so members holding 0, false or null are left out of the output. The wiki documents the default DateFormat as a "\Date(value)" form, not ISO 8601.

The global options (NetJSON.DateFormat, CaseSensitive and others, mostly [Obsolete]) are copied into a [ThreadStatic] NetJSONSettings.CurrentSettings the first time each thread uses it. Changing a static option later does not affect threads that have already serialized, so pass a NetJSONSettings instance instead.
The IncludeFields setter ignores its argument and always sets true, so public fields are serialized along with properties. The wiki still says the default is false.

GenerateTypesInto and GenerateAssembly can save a precompiled DLL only on .NET Framework. On .NET Standard and .NET 5+ the dynamic assembly is run-only, so the first-call IL-generation cost cannot be moved to build time.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No .NET siblings are catalogued in this category: the listed JSON entries (simdjson, yyjson, Sonic, orjson, sonic-rs, etc.) serve C/C++, Go, Rust or Python. NetJSON matters only if you are on .NET and want typed POCO-to-string mapping, not a native parser behind bindings.
verified_claims_summary: The README's ratios are serialization times from a 2014 theburningmonk SimpleSpeedTester run on one small object: NetJson 112.24 ms vs 380.59 ms for Json.NET 6.0.4 (~3.4x). Deserialization was 175.00 vs 437.53 ms (~2.5x), protobuf-net beat NetJSON on both, and no CPU, .NET runtime or build settings were given. The README's '1.6x faster than protobuf-net' comes from a separate undocumented log in which deserialization was a tie (252.18 vs 251.50 ms).
status_note: Active but in single-maintainer bug-fix mode: releases are sporadic, and 1.4.7 (2026-09-05) fixed ISO DateTime formatting (#253, #254). It is MIT-licensed, has ~1.22M NuGet downloads and is easy to add from NuGet, but no UTF-8, Span or Stream support has landed.
